system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2125-03-03 01:48:00 to 2125-03-03 17:14:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, a history of kidney and pancreas transplants, and multiple comorbidities was admitted for peritoneal dialysis catheter placement. She had been on hemodialysis and was holding warfarin in preparation for surgery. The procedure was performed successfully with lysis of peritoneal adhesions and creation of a cutaneoperitoneal fistula. Postoperatively, she had adequate pain control with IV and then oral analgesics, tolerated a regular diet, and ambulated with assistance. Her medications were adjusted, including increasing midodrine to 5 mg twice daily for blood pressure support and restarting warfarin at a reduced dose. She was discharged on postoperative day two to extended care with instructions on incision care, weight monitoring, activity restrictions, and medication management.
problems: Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled
Diabetes with ophthalmic manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted because your INR was very high—9.8—which means your blood is too thin and you’re at risk for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that sounds scary. I didn’t feel any bleeding, though. I just had that sore throat again, like a few months ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned discomfort when swallowing. That’s likely esophagitis, possibly from yeast, especially since you’ve had it before. We’re going to treat that with an antifungal medication called fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but why did my INR go so high? I stopped my Coumadin when it was 6, like they told me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. Even though you stopped Coumadin four days ago, it can stay in your system. Also, your recent peritoneal dialysis catheter placement and possibly your diet or other meds like amiodarone may have contributed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And now with this fluconazole, will that make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fluconazole can increase your INR even more. That’s why we’re not restarting Coumadin for now. You’ll stay off it until your INR is back in the safe range—between 2.0 and 3.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my transplant meds? I’m on tacrolimus and sirolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent point. Fluconazole also affects those levels. We’ll lower your tacrolimus and sirolimus doses starting in two days and check your levels twice a week to keep them safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve also been having some pain in my right hand. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray this morning. Good news—it shows no fracture or dislocation. But we did see vascular calcifications and some bone thinning, which are common with your history of diabetes and kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So nothing broken. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your morning labs just came back. Your INR has improved—from 9.3 down to 4.6. That’s a good drop after the vitamin K you got during dialysis yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? Is it safe to go back to rehab soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you today. Your heart and lungs are stable, your dialysis access is healing well, and you’re feeling better overall. We’ll send you back to extended care with clear instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take fluconazole for two weeks for the esophagitis. Hold off on Coumadin. We’ll reduce your tacrolimus and sirolimus soon. And you must get your INR and transplant drug levels checked twice a week while on fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow up. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Your nurse will go over the written instructions, and you’ll see your specialist soon to review all your meds. Take care, and keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. The nurse changed your PD catheter dressing—looks clean and dry. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been keeping it covered like they told me last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Also, your urine showed some yeast, but the fluconazole will cover that. Just keep an eye out for any new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re alert, walking with your walker, and your vitals are stable. We’re confident you can continue recovering at the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: no Coumadin, take fluconazole daily, and get those blood tests twice a week. Your care team will coordinate the rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got it written down. I’ll follow through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, a history of kidney and pancreas transplants, atrial fibrillation, and multiple comorbidities was admitted due to an elevated INR of 9.8. She had recently undergone peritoneal dialysis catheter placement and had stopped warfarin, but her INR continued to rise. She also reported symptoms of esophagitis, likely candidal, and was started on fluconazole. Her INR improved to 4.6 with vitamin K administration. Medication adjustments included holding warfarin, starting fluconazole, and planning reductions in tacrolimus and sirolimus due to drug interactions. She remained stable, her PD catheter site was healing, and she was discharged back to extended care with instructions for close monitoring of INR and immunosuppressant levels.
